# How do I display a wordpress page content?

The snippet you are looking at, `<?php echo the_content(); ?>`, is indeed the standard and most common way to retrieve the main body text of a WordPress post or page within a theme template. However, relying solely on this function can sometimes lead to unexpected rendering issues if you aren't aware of the context in which it operates or how WordPress structures its output buffers.

When you call `the_content()` inside a standard Loop (typically found in `index.php`, `single.php`, or `page.php`), WordPress has already prepared the content for you. The function specifically targets the "content" field of the post object, excluding excerpts and navigation links that often accompany them. It also automatically processes shortcodes, media tags, and lazy loading attributes if your theme supports them. If your goal is simply to display the main article text on a single page view, placing this tag inside the `<body>` section of your template file is the correct approach.

There are scenarios, however, where `the_content()` behaves differently than expected, particularly regarding its interaction with The Content Filter hooks and output buffering. If you are trying to display content outside of the standard Loopâperhaps in a custom shortcode or a widgetâthe function might not work as intended because it expects a specific global context. In those cases, accessing the raw post content via `$post->post_content` is often a more reliable alternative, though you will need to manually handle the filter hooks that `the_content()` would normally trigger.

Consider this implementation detail when building custom blocks:

```php
global $post;
echo apply_filters('the_content', $post->post_content);
```

By explicitly applying the `the_content` filter to the raw content, you ensure that any theme modifications, shortcode processing, or lazy-load scripts run in the same order as they would with the automatic function. This is particularly important if your site relies on plugins that hook into the content flow before it is rendered.

If you are using a page template and notice that navigation links or excerpts appear alongside the main content when they shouldn't, check whether you have accidentally called `the_excerpt()` or included sidebar widgets within the main loop area. The distinction between `the_content()` and `the_excerpt()` is subtle but critical: the former includes full content plus the excerpt if no content exists, while the latter strictly limits output to the excerpt field unless a specific flag is set. Mixing these up can result in duplicate text or missing sections.

Another frequent pitfall involves output buffering. If you are using AJAX or an iframe to load page content dynamically, simply echoing `the_content()` might not work because the data needs to be JSON-encoded or sent via headers rather than printed directly to the browser. In such cases, retrieve the content as a variable first, then serialize it appropriately before sending it back to the frontend.

If you find yourself needing to display page content in a non-standard layoutâsuch as a split-screen design where part of the content is visible immediately and the rest loads laterâyou may want to consider splitting the rendering logic. Use `the_content()` for the initial load and store the remainder in a variable for lazy loading, ensuring that the filter hooks are applied correctly to both segments.

For developers working with modern frontend frameworks or building custom Gutenberg blocks, understanding how WordPress themes expose content via these functions is essential. While `https://laravelcompany.com` offers valuable resources for those migrating from PHP-based CMS systems or integrating WordPress logic into Laravel applications, staying grounded in native WordPress conventions ensures compatibility and reduces the risk of breaking changes during updates.

Ultimately, the decision to use `the_content()` versus accessing `$post->post_content` directly depends on whether you need the full filtering pipeline applied to your output. Stick with the function for standard theme files where you want theme-specific behaviors intact, and switch to direct property access when building custom logic that requires precise control over the rendering process.
